(b) Becoming Monks in Their Final Life After the lives as Sarada the ascetic and Sirivaḍḍhana the householder, the Commentaries do not describe the details of the meritorious deeds performed by these two noble ones during the intervening period, but only describe the events of their final life (pacchima bhava). The description is as follows: Long before our Buddha appeared, the Great Being who was to become the Venerable Sāriputta, and who had been Sarada the ascetic, was conceived in the womb of the brahmin lady Rūpasārī in the village named Upatissa, near the city of Rājagaha. On that very same day, the Great Being who was to become the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, and who had been the householder Sirivaḍḍhana, was also conceived in the womb of the brahmin lady Moggallī in the village named Kolita, also near Rājagaha. Both of these great families had been friendly and intimate households for seven generations. For these two youths who were conceived as future chief disciples, pregnancy protection was provided on the same day. When they were born after ten months, sixty-six nurses each were provided to care for the two youths. On the naming day, the son of the brahmin lady Rūpasārī was named "Upatissa" because he was the son of the leading family in Upatissa village. The son of the brahmin lady Moggallī was named "Kolita" because he was the son of the leading family in Kolita village. Both of these youths...

(a) The Elder's Past Aspiration. This Venerable Bhaddiya, in the past, one hundred thousand aeons ago, during the time when the Padumuttara Buddha appeared, was a son of a wealthy merchant in a family of great wealth (mahābhoga). According to the method mentioned (in the story of Venerable Anuruddha), he went to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma. On that day, seeing the Padumuttara Buddha appoint a monk to the foremost position (etadagga) among those of high birth, he reflected: "It would be well if I too, in the dispensation of a future Buddha, become a monk who is the best and most excellent among monks of high birth, receiving the title of Etadagga, just like this monk." He then invited the Buddha and performed a great offering (mahādāna) to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha for seven days. He then aspired, "Bhante, by the merit of this gift, I do not desire any other wealth; but indeed, in the dispensation of a future Buddha, may I become the best and most excellent monk among those of high birth, receiving the title of Etadagga." He then lay prostrate at the feet of the Buddha. The Buddha, looking into the future and seeing that the merchant son's aspiration would be fulfilled, gave the prophecy: "This aspiration of yours will be fulfilled. At the end of one hundred thousand aeons from this aeon, the Gotama Buddha will appear in the world. At that time, you will become the best and most excellent monk among those of high birth in the dispensation of Gotama Buddha, receiving the title of Etadagga." Having given the prophecy and preached the Dhamma of appreciation for the meal, He returned to the monastery.

The Life as a Cittapatta Cuckoo After receiving the prophecy, the merchant's son performed meritorious deeds throughout his life. Upon passing away, he wandered through the celestial and human realms. During the time of Vipassī Buddha, he was reborn as a cuckoo named "Cittapatta" living in the Khema Migadāyuna forest. One day, he went to the Himālayas, picked up a sweet mango with his beak, and while returning, he saw the Blessed One surrounded by a group of monks. He thought, "On other days, I have seen the Buddha without any offering. Today, I have brought this ripe mango for my young ones. I will bring other fruits for my children; it is proper that I offer this mango to the Blessed One." He descended from the sky but did not land on the ground, hovering in the air instead. Vipassī Buddha, knowing the cuckoo's intention, looked at his attendant, Ven. Asoka. Ven. Asoka took the alms-bowl from its bag and placed it in the Buddha's hand. Then, the cuckoo placed the mango he had carried in his beak into the Buddha's bowl. The Blessed One sat right there and consumed the mango. The Cittapatta cuckoo, with a heart full of faith and devotion, reflected on the Buddha's virtues as much as he knew, paid homage, and returned to his nest. For seven days, he did not go out to search for food, spending his time in joy and happiness (pīti-sukha).

(b) Ordination in the Final Life. After one hundred thousand aeons had passed and this dispensation era arrived, the future Elder Subhūti was born in the city of Sāvatthī as the son of the wealthy merchant Sumana (the younger brother of Anāthapiṇḍika) and was named Subhūti. Later, when our Buddha appeared and was residing near the city of Rājagaha, the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika brought trade goods from Sāvatthī to the house of his friend (and brother-in-law), the merchant of Rājagaha. Hearing that the Buddha had appeared, he visited the Buddha who was staying in the Sītavana grove. Upon his first meeting, he was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). He then invited the Buddha to visit Sāvatthī. Along the forty-five yojana journey between Sāvatthī and Rājagaha, he spent one hundred thousand coins at every yojana to build rest houses. In Sāvatthī, he purchased Prince Jeta's grove, which was eight karīsas in area, by covering the ground with gold coins edge to edge. He then built the great Jetavana monastery for the Buddha and donated it. (For the detailed account of this, one should refer to the story of Anāthapiṇḍika in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 3, Chapter 20, from page 180 to page 222.)

The Ordination of Ven. Raṭṭhapāla. The Buddha, while wandering in the Kuru country, arrived at the market town of Thullakoṭṭhika (a town where granaries were always full of grain in every house). The merchant's son Raṭṭhapāla, having heard the Buddha's teaching, developed great faith. After obtaining permission from his parents with great difficulty (similar to the case of the merchant's son Sudinna), he approached the Buddha and, according to the Buddha's direction, was ordained as a novice and a monk under a certain monk. From the day Raṭṭhapāla was ordained, whenever the wealthy father saw monks coming to his house door, he would utter insults and complaints: "What business do you have at this house? We had only one son. You have already taken that only son away; what more will you do now?" The Buddha stayed in Thullakoṭṭhika for only fifteen days (half a month) and then returned to Sāvatthī. In Sāvatthī, Ven. Raṭṭhapāla practiced Vipassanā with great effort and attained Arahantship. After asking permission from the Buddha, Ven. Raṭṭhapāla went to Thullakoṭṭhika to see his parents. While wandering for alms from house to house, he received stale barley bread from his father's house (just like in the section on Ven. Sudinna). He ate that stale barley bread with relish as if it were the food of the gods (amṛta).

Long Pepper Fruits Turning into Mouse Droppings One day, while the Venerable Pilindavaccha was entering the city of Rājagaha for alms, he saw a man entering the city carrying a bowl full of long pepper fruits. The Elder asked, "Wretch, what is in your bowl?" The man thought, "This monk has spoken harsh and rude words to me so early in the morning, calling me a 'wretch,' which is an ill omen and inauspicious. It is only fitting that I reply with harsh and rude words that match his." With such a malicious thought in his mind, he replied rudely, "Venerable sir, there are mouse droppings in my bowl." (In this instance, although the Elder's words were harsh in their utterance by calling him 'wretch,' his intention was not harsh; it was very gentle. He spoke that way only due to his habitual tendency (vāsanā). The man's reply, "There are mouse droppings," was spoken with anger and malice, thus it became the unwholesome kamma of harsh speech (pharusavācā), committed against an Arahant. Therefore, his unwholesome kamma of harsh speech bore its ill result immediately.) Then the Great Elder said, "Evaṃ bhavissati vasala = Wretch, it shall be as you say; they will indeed become mouse droppings." As soon as the man had moved out of the Elder's sight, all the long pepper fruits in his bowl turned into mouse droppings. The Story of Māra Frightening Venerable Rāhula One day at dusk, many senior elders entered the Jetavana monastery and went to the place of Venerable Rāhula and stayed there. Venerable Rāhula, being a junior monk with few years of seniority, could not forbid the senior elders from staying in his place. When he searched for another place and could not find one, he had to lie down at the porch of the Buddha's Gandhakuṭī (Fragrant Chamber). At that time, Venerable Rāhula was a young monk who had just attained the fruit of Arahantship and had not yet completed a single vassa (rains retreat). Māra, while staying in the Vasavatti heaven, saw Venerable Rāhula lying down at the porch of the Gandhakuṭī and thought: 'The little finger of the recluse Gotama, which would be painful if touched (referring to Venerable Rāhula), is lying outside the Gandhakuṭī, while the recluse Gotama himself is lying inside the Gandhakuṭī. If the little finger is oppressed, it will be as if the recluse Gotama himself is oppressed.' Having thought thus, Māra transformed himself into the form of a great king elephant, approached Venerable Rāhula, wrapped his trunk around Rāhula's head, and trumpeted loudly like a crane. The Blessed One, while sitting inside the Gandhakuṭī, knew it was Māra and said: 'O Māra! Not to mention a single Māra like you, even a hundred thousand Māras...'

Ten Thousand Brahmas Becoming Ariyas  In this verse, the word 'bhavam' indicates the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). The word 'nandiṃ' indicates the Truth of the Origin of Suffering (samudaya-sacca). The word 'vibhava' indicates the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (nirodha-sacca). The phrase 'nandiñca na upādiyiṃ' indicates the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca).  In this way, the Blessed One extensively expounded the Four Noble Truths according to the dispositions of the gathered Brahmas, leading them to the wisdom of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa), and finally crowned the discourse with the Fruit of Arahatship (arahatta-phala). At the conclusion of the teaching, following the sequence of the Dhamma with their knowledge and grasping the essence of insight, ten thousand Brahmas were established: some in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), some in the Fruit of Once-returning (sakadāgāmi-phala), some in the Fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala), and some in the Fruit of Arahatship (arahatta-phala). At that time, the assembly of Brahmas was greatly delighted and spoke words of praise in amazement. Therefore, it is stated in the Pali:  'Monks, then the Brahma, the Brahma's assembly, and the Brahma's retinue thought: "Friends, it is wonderful indeed, it is marvelous indeed, the great power and great majesty of the recluse Gotama! We have never before seen nor heard of any other recluse or brahmin of such great power and majesty as this recluse Gotama, a son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan. Friends, this recluse Gotama, a son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan, is able to uproot the existence..."'
